title: Married and single (1 Corinthians 7)
hook: Paul answers their questions practically, honoring both marriage and singleness
tomorrow: you're right about the facts. is that the end of it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body as a temple, bought with a price. The line: glorify God in your body.

An advice column. An anonymous question box. A group chat full of 'asking for a friend.' Paul gets the old version: "Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me". The Corinthians have mailed him their questions, and the first ones are about marriage, sex and staying single. Chapter seven reads like half a phone call: we hear Paul's answers and have to guess the questions.
screen: `ASKING FOR A FRIEND.` → `THE THINGS WHEREOF YE WROTE.` → `HALF A PHONE CALL.`

segments.voice: Today's question: is a single life a lesser life? Paul answers personally: "For I would that all men were even as I myself." He seems to be unmarried, and content. But he won't make it a rule: "But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that." Marriage is a gift. Singleness is a gift. Neither is the backup plan. And he's careful about whose voice is speaking: on divorce, "I command, yet not I, but the Lord"; on another question, "I have no commandment of the Lord: yet I give my judgment". A neighbor tradition keeps two honored ways of life too. In Buddhism, monks and nuns leave home for the path, and the Buddha also taught householders. In the Sigalovada Sutta he tells a young man how a husband honors his wife, with respect, courtesy and faithfulness, and how she cares for him and the household in return. That's shared ground: a vowed single life and a married life, each with its place. The honest difference is the reason. For Paul, singleness frees undivided attention for the Lord, and both ways are a gift of God. The Buddhist monk or nun leaves home to let go of craving on the way to nirvana.
screen: `IS SINGLE A LESSER LIFE?` · `EACH HAS HIS PROPER GIFT.` · `THE BUDDHA TAUGHT HOUSEHOLDERS TOO.` · `TWO WAYS, DIFFERENT REASONS.` · then, large: `EACH HAS HIS GIFT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind three people whose lives look different from yours: married, single, widowed, still waiting. For each, count one honest gift you see in their life, without measuring it against your own. Let each gift stay as it is, theirs and good.
Married and single. Two ways of life Paul answers in one chapter, and calls both a gift.
The line to keep: each has his gift, one after this manner, another after that. Go in peace.

howItsDone: Christians read 1 Corinthians 7 in different ways: Catholic and Orthodox churches draw on it in honoring vowed single life, and other churches turn to it in teaching on marriage and singleness.

chat.meaning: Paul says every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, another after that. Singleness and marriage are both gifts.

Sigalovada Sutta.meaning: a Buddhist discourse on the duties of household life

householders.meaning: people who live at home with families, not as monks

nirvana.meaning: in Buddhism, the end of craving and suffering

Corinthians.meaning: members of the church at Corinth

notes: Recipe v3, wisdom shape with the unity thread: the question (is a single life a lesser life?), Paul's answer (both are a gift, 7:7), and one neighbor: Buddhism's two honored ways (monastics who leave home; householders), with the Sigalovada Sutta (Digha Nikaya 31) paraphrased: a husband honors his wife with respect, courtesy and faithfulness, and she cares for him and the household. Honest difference: the reason (Paul: undivided attention for the Lord, both a gift of God; the monastic: letting go of craving toward nirvana). Please have a Buddhist reviewer confirm the paraphrase and that the difference is fair; nothing ranked.
The index carry is 'each has his gift'; the KJV of 7:7 reads 'every man hath his proper gift of God'. Kept as the index has it.
'He seems to be unmarried' rests on 7:7–8; kept hedged. 'singleness frees undivided attention for the Lord' paraphrases 7:32–34.
The lesson names divorce only as a topic Paul marks as the Lord's command; it does not teach on divorce, where churches differ widely.
